Nov 20, 2026

CVE pages in Zero Wire

Radar

Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire ↗︎ now has a page for every published CVE. Each page brings together what you need to decide how urgently to act on a vulnerability: how severe it is, whether it is being exploited, what it affects, and how to fix it.

Browse CVEs

The CVE list ↗︎ includes every published CVE. Sort them by date or CVSS score, search by CVE ID or keyword, such as a product or vendor name, and filter by severity and year. Each row shows the CVE's score and highlights CVEs in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog and those with a fix available.

CVE pages

Each CVE page, such as CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell) ↗︎, starts with its CVSS score, description, and key dates, followed by:

  • Exploitation: whether the CVE is in the CISA KEV catalog, including known ransomware use, the CISA SSVC assessment, and the FIRST EPSS probability of exploitation.
  • Affected products: the affected vendors, products, and versions, as listed by the organization that published the CVE and by NVD.
  • Recommended actions: how to fix the vulnerability, or reduce the risk until you can, including CISA's guidance for known exploited CVEs.
  • Severity: every CVSS score for the CVE, with each metric explained.
  • Weaknesses and attack patterns: the related CWE weaknesses and CAPEC attack patterns.
  • References: advisories, patches, and other sources.

CVEs cited in Zero Wire briefings ↗︎ link to their CVE pages, and each CVE page links back to the briefings that cite it.

Search and follow

Search for a CVE ID or keyword from anywhere on Radar, using the search bar or Cmd+K (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux), to jump straight to a CVE page.

To follow new CVEs, subscribe to the RSS ↗︎, Atom ↗︎, or JSON ↗︎ feed. Each feed can be filtered by severity, such as the feed of Critical CVEs ↗︎.

Explore the CVE list ↗︎ on Cloudflare Radar.

Nov 19, 2026

Autonomous system types on Cloudflare Radar

Radar

Cloudflare Radar now shows the type of each autonomous system (AS): Access ISP, Hosting/Cloud/Content, or Organization. AS types are inferred automatically, so an individual AS can be misclassified. They make it easier to tell, for example, whether traffic or attacks come from residential and mobile networks or from data centers.

  • Access ISP (ACCESS_ISP): networks that connect end users, such as home broadband and mobile operators, plus transit providers.
  • Hosting/Cloud/Content (HOSTING_CLOUD_CONTENT): hosting providers, cloud platforms, and content delivery networks.
  • Organization (ORGANIZATION): enterprises, universities, governments, banks, and IXP route servers.

ASes without a type are shown as Unclassified. To report a wrong AS type, email radar@cloudflare.com.

Top ASes by HTTP traffic in Portugal ↗︎, with the type of each AS shown before its number.

Radar pages

  • AS pages, such as AS7922 ↗︎, show the AS type in the AS information card.
  • An icon before the AS number shows its type across Radar. Hover over the icon to see the AS type.
  • The Data Explorer ↗︎ can break down and filter HTTP, NetFlows, DNS, and layer 7 attack data by AS type.

The AS type in the AS7922 ↗︎ information card.

Worldwide HTTP requests by AS type over the last four weeks, from the Data Explorer ↗︎.

API

  • The Get AS details, List ASes, and Get AS details by IP address endpoints return a new category field with the AS type, or null when the AS is not classified.
  • The HTTP, NetFlows, DNS, and layer 7 attacks endpoints accept a new asCategory filter, and their summary and timeseries groups endpoints support a new AS_CATEGORY dimension. Both accept ACCESS_ISP, HOSTING_CLOUD_CONTENT, ORGANIZATION, and UNCLASSIFIED, where UNCLASSIFIED also covers traffic that could not be mapped to an AS. For HTTP, they are supported for date ranges starting on or after 2023-05-01.
  • The global search endpoint returns an entity with details of the matched AS, including its category, for AS results, and of the matched region for region (adm1 and adm2) results.

For example, to get the share of HTTP requests by AS type in the last week:

Visit an AS page ↗︎ on Cloudflare Radar to see its type, or read the AS type definitions.

Nov 9, 2026

Redesigned Bots Directory on Cloudflare Radar, now powered by BotBase

Radar

The Cloudflare Radar Bots Directory ↗︎ now uses BotBase, Cloudflare's catalog of the bots and agents it tracks, and has a new design matching the Radar homepage.

Each bot page has a new Identity section showing the bot's access level, content use, Web Bot Auth verification, and user agents. Bot operators are also searchable from the Radar site search.

API

The List bots and Get bot details endpoints now describe each bot with:

  • categories: a bot can now have more than one category. Categories follow BotBase's groups, which add COMMERCE, and some older categories are now part of broader groups.
  • accessLevel: DIRECT if the bot reaches websites under its own identity, or INTERMEDIARY if it acts on behalf of another agent or a person.
  • contentUse: full if the content it fetches is kept and reused (for example, for model training or a search index), reference if it is cited or linked back to the source, or immediate if it is used once to answer a user's request.
  • documentationUrl and operatorWebsiteUrl (bot details only).

category and operatorUrl are deprecated in favor of categories and documentationUrl.

Visit the Bots Directory ↗︎ on Cloudflare Radar.

Nov 3, 2026

Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities

Radar

Cloudflare Radar now includes Zero Wire ↗︎, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities and threats. Each briefing separates confirmed facts from open questions, lists remediation steps, and shows what Cloudflare observes about the threat.

Briefings

Briefings are grouped by urgency. Needs attention covers active incidents, new guidance, or unresolved scope that security teams should review now. Reference keeps stable briefings available, even if not every affected system has been patched. Each card shows the recommended action and summarizes what happened, why it matters, and what to do.

Each briefing page expands on the card with an update chronology and an overview, followed by:

  • What to do now: remediation steps, plus a prompt to copy into an AI agent with access to your infrastructure, asking for an evidence-based assessment of affected systems and exposure.
  • Cloudflare coverage: the Cloudflare products that protect against the threat, and any impact on Cloudflare's own services.
  • Evidence and sources: vendor advisories, CVE records, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, and Radar charts, such as requests matching the related Cloudflare WAF rules.

Follow updates

Search briefings by CVE, name, or tag, or browse every briefing with a given tag. To follow new briefings and updates, subscribe to the Zero Wire RSS feed ↗︎ or to the feed of a single tag. New briefings also appear in the Caught on Radar ↗︎ section of the Radar homepage.

Send questions or feedback from any briefing page, or at radar@cloudflare.com.

For more details, read the blog post ↗︎ or visit Zero Wire ↗︎.

Oct 30, 2026

Cloudflare WAN supports regional Gateway HTTP inspection

Data Localization SuiteCloudflare WANCloudflare One

Cloudflare WAN traffic can now use a Gateway processing region with Regional Services. HTTPS traffic enters a Cloudflare data center (that may be outside the selected region) via an IPsec or GRE tunnel, or through Direct CNI, and remains encrypted until Gateway forwards it to the selected region for TLS decryption and HTTP inspection. This feature gives organizations control over where their sensitive traffic is processed, supporting their data sovereignty goals.

This feature requires unified routing. The processing region applies to Gateway HTTP traffic and does not apply to Gateway DNS or network policy processing.

Contact your account team to configure a processing region. For supported regions, configuration details, and limitations, refer to Data residency for Cloudflare One.

It shows your Regional Services, Customer Metadata Boundary, and Geo Key Manager settings in one place, so you no longer need to check several dashboard pages and APIs to see where your traffic is processed and where your logs and private keys are stored.

To find it, go to Application Security > Data Localization Suite, or search for "DLS" in the dashboard.

The Overview has a tab for each product:

  • Regional Services: regionalized hostnames (filter by region or zone), regionalized IP bindings, and regionalized Spectrum applications, each with its region.
  • Customer Metadata Boundary: whether the boundary is on, the region (US or EU), and whether out-of-region access is allowed.
  • Geo Key Manager: every custom certificate with a geo policy, with its hostname, zone, region, and status.

Each item links to the dashboard page where you change its setting, and each tab links to the product's documentation.

To learn more, refer to the Data Localization Suite documentation.

Oct 27, 2026

SQL API introspection: `include_attributes` parameter

Analytics

The SQL API introspection endpoint has a new include_attributes query parameter. Setting it to true discovers the keys of a dataset's attributes JSON column, and their types, from the preceding seven days of your account's data. Discovered keys are returned in the dataset's attributes response field.

Some datasets store additional key-value data in an attributes JSON column, which you query with exact-key lookups such as attributes['http.method']. The previous way to discover these keys, include_custom_attributes, returned names in a custom_attributes field. The new names make it clearer that each returned name is a key you access through the attributes column.

include_custom_attributes and custom_attributes are deprecated but still work. Update integrations to use include_attributes and attributes.

For more information, refer to Attributes.

Oct 13, 2026

Deeper Core Web Vitals Diagnostics: LCP & INP Sub-Part Metrics in Real User Monitoring

Cloudflare Web Analytics

The Core Web Vitals tell you whether a page is slow but beyond perceived load time, layout instability, or responsiveness they do not guide you to the problematic area directly. To help you with this, Real User Monitoring (RUM) in Web Analytics now breaks Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) into their respective sub-parts. It also splits connection time into TCP and TLS. You can see this visualised in the dashboard or query it through the GraphQL Analytics API.

LCP sub-parts

LCP is broken into four phases, so you can see which one is impacting your perceived load time:

  1. Time to First Byte: how long the browser waits for the HTML document (timeToFirstByte in GraphQL).
  2. Resource load delay: how long the browser takes to discover the LCP resource after the document starts arriving (lcpResourceLoadDelay).
  3. Resource load duration: how long it takes to download that resource (lcpResourceLoadTime).
  4. Element render delay: the gap between the resource arriving and the element appearing on screen (lcpElementRenderDelay).

You do not have to remember all this detail, there are tooltips available to guide you next to each sub-part metric in the dashboard.

INP sub-parts

INP is broken into three phases, guiding you to the area slowing down responsiveness:

  1. Input delay: how long an interaction (click, tap or key press) is blocked before it can be processed (inpInputDelay).
  2. Processing duration: how long your event handlers take to run (inpProcessingDuration).
  3. Presentation delay: how long the browser takes to render the next frame after the handlers finish (inpPresentationDelay).

TCP and TLS timing

The page load timing breakdown now separates connection setup from the TLS handshake, so you can tell a slow network path from a slow TLS negotiation:

  • Connection time (excluding TLS) (connectionTimeWithoutTLS)
  • TLS handshake time: (tlsTime).

Note: we've retained connectionTime in the GraphQL API so you can still analyze the combined time.

How to query the GraphQL data

The sub-parts are available on rumWebVitalsEventsAdaptiveGroups as percentiles, for example: lcpResourceLoadDelayP50 or inpInputDelayP50. The connection split is available on rumPerformanceEventsAdaptiveGroups as connectionTimeWithoutTLSP50 and tlsTimeP50, and so on for the other percentiles.

The percentiles available are: P25, P50, P75, P90, P95, P99, P999. All values are in microseconds. A negative value means the data is not available.

How to get started

Go to Real user monitoring ↗

Head to the 'Core Web Vitals' section, here you can scroll down the report to see the sub-parts. The 'Page Load' section contains the Connection and TLS negotiation durations.

For more on the data, refer to the Web Analytics docs and the GraphQL Analytics API docs.

30 days of analytics data on every plan

Analytics

Every plan now gets at least 30 days of analytics data. Adaptive analytics datasets, such as HTTP requests, security events, and DNS analytics, retain at least 31 days of data for Free and Pro domains, and you can query up to 30 days in a single request. Previously, Free and Pro domains could see between 24 hours and 8 days of history depending on the dataset.

A full month of history lets you investigate an issue after it happens, compare today with the same day in previous weeks, and tell a one-time spike from a longer trend. The change applies in the Cloudflare dashboard, in Custom Dashboards, and through the GraphQL Analytics API.

Domain analytics also now live in one place. In the Cloudflare dashboard, select a domain and go to Analytics to see Traffic, Performance, Security, Cache, Origin, DNS, and Visitors as tabs that share one time range and one set of filters. Account-level analytics are under Observability > Analytics.

This change does not alter which datasets or fields your plan can access. Aggregated datasets, such as httpRequests1hGroups, keep their existing per-plan limits. To check the exact retention and query window for a zone or account, query the settings for each dataset.

Oct 2, 2026

SQL API (Beta)

Analytics

The SQL API is now available in beta. It provides a single HTTP endpoint for querying Cloudflare analytics and observability data using SQL. Supported dataset types include event datasets (such as HTTP requests and security events), state datasets (such as D1 storage), log datasets (such as Workers logs), and Workers Analytics Engine datasets.

The SQL API supports SELECT queries with filtering, aggregation, LIKE, CASE, BETWEEN, IS NULL, and ordering. Adaptively sampled datasets apply sample weights automatically for COUNT, SUM, and AVG. You can also query from a Cloudflare Worker using the Workers binding without managing an API token.

The SQL API powers Monitors and is available for direct querying on all plans.

For syntax, datasets, and limits, refer to SQL API.

Analytics

You can now build Custom Dashboards charts from Workers Observability data. Two new datasets, Workers Observability — Logs and Workers Observability — Traces (OTel), let you chart Worker invocations, log levels, errors, CPU and wall time, span counts, and durations next to HTTP traffic, security events, and other analytics datasets.

Aug 24, 2026

RPKI ASPA path validation on Cloudflare Radar

Radar

Radar adds an ASPA validation tool ↗︎ to its Routing section ↗︎. Enter a BGP AS_PATH and the tool checks it against the Autonomous System Provider Authorization (ASPA) ↗︎ records currently published in the RPKI, returning a verdict of Valid, Invalid, or Unknown. An Invalid verdict means no chain of provider authorizations covers the whole path, which is the signature of a route leak.

Validation follows draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification ↗︎, so verdicts match those produced by validators implementing the same draft. The draft is still a work in progress and not yet an RFC.

Enter a path

Paths are read in BGP wire order: the rightmost AS is the origin, and the leftmost AS is the one closest to the collector or router that observed the route. AS numbers can be separated by spaces, commas, or hyphens, with or without an AS prefix. The full ASPA snapshot is loaded into the browser once, so the verdict, graph, and trace update as the path is edited, with no further requests. A set of example paths covers the interesting cases, including a route leak with an AS0 ASPA, where an AS declares that it has no providers at all.

Choose an algorithm

The draft defines two verification algorithms that differ only in whether a down-ramp is permitted:

  • Upstream (section 5.4 ↗︎) — for routes received from a customer, peer, route server client, or route server. Only an up-ramp is permitted.
  • Downstream (section 5.5 ↗︎) — for routes received from a provider. Both an up-ramp and a down-ramp are permitted.

An up-ramp is the run of consecutive customer-to-provider hops from the origin to the apex of the path, and a down-ramp is the equivalent run from the announcing neighbor back to that apex. The tool evaluates both algorithms at once and labels each with its verdict, so a path that is legitimate when received from one session type and a leak when received from another is visible without switching modes. Selecting an algorithm drives the graph and the trace.

Read the result

The ASPA validation graph draws the path hop by hop, labeling each AS with its role, whether it publishes an ASPA, and how many providers that ASPA authorizes. Every hop is marked Provider+, Not Provider+, or No attestation, and the maximum and minimum bounds of each ramp are drawn against the length of the path. Hops that no ramp reaches are highlighted, because a path the ramps cannot cover end to end is Invalid. The accompanying ASPA records table lists every AS in the path with its ASPA status and its authorized providers, each linked to its Radar AS page.

Follow the algorithm

The Algorithm step by step section shows the derivation rather than just the answer. Two columns run the same scans under different stopping rules: the upper bounds, which test for Invalid and stop only on Not Provider+, and the lower bounds, which test for Unknown and also stop on No Attestation. A hop is Not Provider+ when the AS publishes an ASPA that does not list the next AS as a provider, and No Attestation when the AS publishes no ASPA at all. Each column lists the outcome for every hop scanned, marks where the scan stopped, gives the resulting ramp length, and then evaluates the verdict rule with the numbers filled in.

Share a validation

The path and the selected algorithm are kept in the URL, so a link reproduces a result exactly — for example, this route leak with an AS0 ASPA ↗︎. Appending &mode=upstream pins the link to the upstream algorithm. The graph is a standard Radar widget, so it can also be embedded or shared as an image.

The records behind the tool are the same ones served by the /bgp/rpki/aspa/snapshot endpoint of the ASPA API, and the number of records loaded and the snapshot timestamp are shown alongside the input.

Try the ASPA validation tool ↗︎ with a path of your own.

Aug 21, 2026

Web Analytics improves soft navigation measurement for Single Page Applications (SPAs)

Cloudflare Web Analytics

Cloudflare Web Analytics (Real User Monitoring) is rolling out accuracy improvements to client-side soft navigations. Update: this update is complete as of 2026-09-04.

This change may alter the volume of reported pageviews and visits in the dashboard and GraphQL API. The reported Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) metric may also fluctuate. The extent of these variances depend on your front-end architecture and visitor traffic patterns.

Single Page Applications (SPAs)—such as websites built with React, Angular, Vue, or Svelte—predominantly use soft navigations. Soft navigations avoid fully unloading the current page and rendering the next one from scratch as visitors navigate.

Any client-side navigation counts as a soft navigation, including navigations intercepted by the Navigation API ↗︎ or triggered by the History API ↗︎. This means a non-SPA website can have soft navigation activity if its implementation uses these APIs.

The main improvement comes from Google Chrome's new Soft Navigation API ↗︎. It natively measures Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) on soft navigations, removing a blind spot in perceived loading speed across pageviews.

We've extended our navigationType values to segment these different types of navigations:

navigationType New? Description
navigate ❌ Hard navigations that traditional websites (or "Multi Page Applications") perform when clicking links or submitting forms
soft-navigation ✅ Where the new Soft Navigation API ↗︎ is available and a visitor makes a client-side navigation, we record these events
routing-apis ✅ Where the native Soft Navigation API is unavailable (e.g. Safari, Firefox, older Chromium-based browsers), we fallback to measuring soft navigations using the Navigation API ↗︎ or History API ↗︎. We cannot collect LCP for these, but the other Core Web Vitals are present.

Prior to this change, we only used History API and all navigations were bucketed into navigate.

For more information, refer to the Navigation Types and Web Analytics SPA documentation pages.

  • Magic BGP Logs: A new dataset with fields including Direction, EventData, EventKind, EventTimestamp, TunnelID, and TunnelName.

Updated fields in existing datasets

  • Firewall events (added): AISecurityCustomTopicCategories, WAFRequestSignatureCategories, and WAFRequestSignatureRefs.
  • Gateway HTTP (added): ExperimentalFeatures and PackageInfo.
  • HTTP requests (added): AISecurityCustomTopicCategories, ClientTLSKeyExchangeGroup, WAFRequestSignatureCategories, and WAFRequestSignatureRefs.

For the complete field definitions for each dataset, refer to Logpush datasets.
